The Complete Plus-Minus (CPM) emerges as a refined statistical construct designed to isolate individual player influence within the complex dynamics of hockey. It leverages logistic regression to model binary outcomes—goals scored for or against—using on-ice event predictors. This dual-logistic approach allows for nuanced estimation of player value beyond traditional plus-minus metrics. The derivation hinges upon the assumption that goal-scoring behavior can be approximated by a probabilistic function of observed actions. As such, CPM operates under a Bayesian paradigm where prior beliefs about player ability inform posterior distributions over performance. Its failure mode arises when data sparsity or non-stationarity undermines model stability. In GSI, this translates into risk-adjusted forecasts of player efficacy, while in GSE, it enables simulation of strategic state transitions through shift-based event sequences. The interplay between these constructs reveals a duality: CPM as a static attribution kernel and shift sequences as a dynamic evolution operator, both grounded in empirical observables yet abstracted into formal mathematical frameworks.
